headline: High: shared MCP/tooling and broad network egress create default data-leak and cascading-action risks between open-agent and open-webui.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents expose MCP/tooling surfaces and can ingest external content; agent_a uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks, while agent_b supports MCP, OpenAPI tool servers, and plugins. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path if one agent forwards untrusted content to the other. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards browser or file content into agent_b tool calls without sanitization
IF agent_b treats agent_a-produced text as instructions inside MCP or plugin prompts
mitigations: Disable automatic forwarding between agents
Add a strict allowlist for tool-call arguments
Strip instructions from copied content before handoff
Require human review before any MCP action
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to inter-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a handles provider auth prompts, session history, project code, and AGENTS.md/README.md, while agent_b touches documents, notes, files, API keys, and persistent memory. Both have broad network egress and cloud/API integrations, so a shared workspace or handoff can expose sensitive data to external services by default. The pairwise leakage path is credible even without a documented shared filesystem.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or mounted volume
IF agent_b is configured to index or upload files from that workspace
IF agent_a forwards session history or auth prompts into external APIs
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mounts per agent
Turn off file indexing/upload in agent_b
Avoid placing secrets in shared directories
Review outbound API destinations for both agents
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss prevention rules

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent_a supports multiple instances with per-installation sessions and can spawn subprocesses; agent_b supports multiple instances with persistent shared web-app sessions and Redis-backed shared state. If both write to the same mutable resources, conflicts can corrupt state or overwrite work. The profiles do not prove a shared directory or git repo, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same filesystem path, database, or git checkout
IF agent_b is deployed with shared Redis state and agent_a also mutates the same artifacts
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Avoid concurrent writes to the same repo
Serialize edits with a simple lock file
Run one agent read-only during the other's write phase
requires-engineering: add resource-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a can produce browser-derived or tool-derived content, and agent_b has broad tool/plugin/MCP capabilities plus persistent memory. If agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or stored memory, amplifying a single bad inference into persistent or externalized mistakes. The interaction is plausible in default tool-heavy setups, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests agent_a output without verification
IF agent_b writes agent_a-derived claims into persistent memory or external tools
IF agent_a's browser/tool output is used as a source of truth
mitigations: Require citation checks before acting on agent_a output
Keep agent_b in review-only mode for agent_a outputs
Disable automatic memory writes from inter-agent handoffs
Add a second-pass verifier for factual claims
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating on downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_a handles provider auth prompts and installation/session data, while agent_b handles API keys, persistent memory, and files. Both are open-source and docs-only, but their storage and retention surfaces differ enough that a shared data class could be retained or logged inconsistently. No specific residency or certification mismatch is documented, so this remains medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in agent_b persistent memory while agent_a logs session history
IF the deployment requires deletion/export guarantees across both agents
mitigations: Do not store regulated data in either agent
Review retention settings before use
Separate logs from user content
Document which agent owns deletion requests
requires-engineering: align retention and export workflows
